 UT Press releases first children’s picture book ‘My Magic Tux’
 Cassidy Gaspard , Staff Writer 
 October 27, 2026 
 Ethan Garnier The Big Orange Tux is on display at the Graduate Hotel on Oct. 21. 
 During the 1998 Fiesta Bowl national championship game, one fan in particular stood out from the Neyland crowd. J.R. Greene, a graduate student, sported a white tuxedo colored with orange marker, orange gloves and an orange top hat.
 When ESPN’s College GameDay’s Chris Fowler invited him onto the field, Greene introduced himself with an iconic message that would kickstart his legacy.
 “I’m J.R. Greene, the Big Orange Tux Guy, and I’m here to show that Tennessee has class,” Greene said.
 Nearly 30 years later, Greene has turned his superfan story into “ My Magic Tux ,” the University of Tennessee Press’s first children’s picture book. He says that initial message is something he still stands by.
 “That’s what I stood for,” Greene said. “It was authentic. It was original. It was true.”
 One Special Teacher
 AfterESPN published an article about his story, Greene was invited to wear the tuxedo to a tailgate and interact with fans. An elementary school teacher approached him and suggested that his story would make a great children’s book about courage and confidence.
 “I began to think, ‘Yes, it actually is a story.’ I see where the elementary school teacher was coming from with the idea of telling children to take risks, put yourself out there,” Greene said. “If you want to grow, you have to be able to put yourself in positions to learn from mistakes and keep going. Then, you can pursue your own dream.”
 Although Greene entertained the idea, he had no idea how to write a children’s book.
 He turned to the internet for research, exploring routes of self-publishing, commercial publishing and academic publishing. He even spoke with the chief operating officer of Simon & Schuster, a New York publishing company, to learn more about the industry.
 “At the time, I didn’t know the University of Tennessee had a press or a publishing office,” Greene said.
 That was until one fateful day in Nashville, when Greene ran into Joe Mazer, dean of the UT College of Communication and Information, who connected him with Katie Hannah, director ofUT Press.
 Tuxie Comes to Life
 Hannah had already considered starting a children’s book line of her own. Greene’s idea, combined with his dedication, presented an opportunity to explore that possibility.
 “His story was so quirky and his enthusiasm so infectious. I was immediately intrigued,” Hannah said. “But he was well prepared, too — he had already hired a co-author and an illustrator, and he was ready to get down to work.”
 Greene’s story was a perfect match for the UT Press, fitting both of their goals to represent the university and give back to greater Tennessee.
 “There are a lot of stories out there, but I wanted to be sure anything that we published fit with the press’s mission to improve the quality of life for the people of Tennessee, and with the university’s land-grant mission to serve lifelong learners,” Hannah said. “My Magic Tux was a slam dunk in that regard.”
 Working alongside co-author Joe Shands and illustrator Nicholas Child, Greene brought his story to life on the page and created his own mascot, Tuxie. After two years of peer review and international Zoom calls from Nashville, to Santa Fe, to England, the wording and imagery became finalized, and Tuxie was ready to hit the shelves.
 Like a football game, “My Magic Tux” is split into two halves. The book also features a specific font designed to help readers with dyslexia.
 “You have to give UT Press a big nod because that was their idea, and that just made the book even more special,” Greene said.
 The publishing process also opened a new door for UT Press, providing a new experience to apply to future publications and possibly more children’s books.
 “We learned so much,” Hannah said. “From composing and editing the book to collaborating with design, production, and marketing and promotion, along with engaging a public relations firm for the first time, I feel like we gained valuable information that we can use not only on future children’s books, but also on all the books we publish.”
 Magical Partnerships
 In true volunteer spirit, “My Magic Tux” has sparked partnerships with local businesses and organizations across Tennessee to promote Greene’s goal to expand access and literacy across Tennessee.
 Through his partnership with the nonprofit UT Press, proceeds from the book go back to UT Libraries. Greene has also donated his proceeds to the university.
 “The UT Press and I would hope that over time, every child that’s a Tennessee Vol fan has an opportunity to get this book,” Greene said. “One of the biggest pieces is access.”
 Bookstores in Knoxville and Nashville, including Alumni Hall, Union Ave Books and Parnassus Books, have also helped make the book available to readers.
 The Knoxville Smokies invited the Tuxie mascot to throw the first pitch at a game, while Cruze Farm created a specialty ice cream flavor called “Tuxie Swirl” and offered signed copies of the book at its store.
 Toyota Material Handling MidSouth donated 500 copies of the book to Knox County schools and libraries.
 Greene said the donated books arrived at schools in boxes labeled with teachers’ last names.
 “It was adorable,” Greene said.
 Remembering the Journey
 Greene’s story is continuing to reach audiences beyond Tennessee. He has held storytimes, book signings, and has appeared on radio shows and in magazine features across the country, a future he never expected to come from a homemade tuxedo.
 “If you go back to when I put that tux on, I had no idea where my day was going to turn,” Greene said. “But 28 years later, here I am with a wonderful book and a storyline and able to speak back to students across the University of Tennessee, so it’s very exciting.”
 With hopes of making “My Magic Tux” a New York Times bestseller, Greene continues to look toward the future while reminding others of the importance of appreciating the entire process.
 “Remember the journey,” Greene said. “When you have that goal out there, set the goal, and pursue it. Win, fail, but continue to learn and enjoy that journey.”
 The experience has also encouraged Greene to pursue more opportunities in his own career and find new ways to give back to the university that guided him along the way.
 “The storyline of the book came through in real life,” Greene said. “I began to pursue different roles, and now I’m beginning to do a lot more mentoring. I want to give back to the University with this book, and I think there’s a lot more exciting journeys ahead.”
 The book’s lessons transcend football and generations. Hannah emphasized the connection reading can bring.
 “This is a book about courage and confidence, about being polite and honest and kind while still jumping at opportunity,” Hannah said. “We hope that people will take these lessons to heart but also have a great time reading the book together.”
 For Greene, the true takeaway reflects the moment that started it all: standing out, taking a chance and being willing to lead.
 “When people ask you if you’re here to lead the team on the field, whatever you’re doing out there, the answer is yes,” Greene said.
 Readers can purchase “My Magic Tux” on the UT Press website .
